teaser: His father died still waiting for a Prophet he was sure he would never meet. The son lived to meet him.
quran_mention: «مَا كَانَ إِبْرَاهِيمُ يَهُودِيًّا وَلَا نَصْرَانِيًّا وَلَكِن كَانَ حَنِيفًا مُّسْلِمًا» — 'Ibrahim was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was upright in faith, submitted to Allah' (Aal Imran 3:67). This is the description Sa'id's father spent his life trying to live by, without a Book and without a teacher.

layers.title: Who He Was
layers.subtitle: Two families bound twice by marriage
layers.content:
Sa'id ibn Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl ibn Abd al-Uzza, of Banu Adi ibn Ka'b — the smallest of the Quraysh clans, and the one that also produced Umar ibn al-Khattab. Nufayl was Umar's grandfather and Sa'id's great-grandfather, so the two men were close kin before they were anything else. Sa'id's kunya was Abu al-A'war and his mother was Fatima bint Ba'ja, of Khuza'a.

He was tall, dark-skinned, with a great deal of hair. He wore a ring with an ayah of the Book of Allah cut into it.

The two households were then tied twice more. Sa'id married a daughter of al-Khattab, Umar's own sister — Ibn Sa'd records her name as Ramla, called Umm Jamil. And Sa'id's sister Atika bint Zayd married Umar and bore him a son, Iyad.

But the fact that shaped Sa'id was none of this. It was his father. Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl had spent his adult life refusing the religion of his own city and looking for a better one, and Sa'id grew up inside that refusal.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: A father who searched, a son who arrived
layers.content:
Zayd ibn Amr went to Syria and questioned the Jews and Christians about religion, and liked neither. A Christian told him what he was already doing: you are holding to the religion of Ibrahim — Allah alone, no partner, and no eating of what is slaughtered to idols. Zayd answered, 'This is what I know, and I follow that religion. The worship of stone or hewn wood is nothing.'

Back in Makkah, Hujayr ibn Abi Ihab watched him wait for the sun to decline, then turn to the Ka'ba and pray two rak'ats: this is the qibla of Ibrahim and Isma'il. Asma bint Abi Bakr saw him with his back against the Ka'ba telling Quraysh that not one of them was on the religion of Ibrahim but him. He bought infant girls out of the pits their fathers had dug: do not kill her, I will support her for you.

He told Amir ibn Rabi'a he was waiting for a Prophet from the children of Isma'il, did not expect to meet him, and asked Amir to greet him for him. Zayd died five years before the Revelation came. His son Sa'id became Muslim before the Prophet ﷺ had even entered the house of al-Arqam to call people.
layers.source: Reported from Amir ibn Rabi'a, Hujayr ibn Abi Ihab and Asma bint Abi Bakr — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: An answer about his father, then Umar
layers.content:
Umar and Sa'id went together to the Prophet ﷺ and asked him about Zayd ibn Amr. He said: may Allah forgive Zayd ibn Amr and have mercy on him — he died on the religion of Ibrahim. Ibn Sa'd notes that from that day the Muslims did not mention Zayd's name without asking mercy for him. Asked about him another time, the Prophet ﷺ called him a single nation who will be raised on the Day of Rising. And when Amir ibn Rabi'a became Muslim he passed on the greeting he had been carrying for years. The Prophet ﷺ returned it, prayed for mercy on Zayd, and said he had seen him in the Garden drawing a bucket.

The other scene in this house is famous without Sa'id usually being named in it. Umar set out to kill the Prophet ﷺ and was turned aside with a question: why not start with your own family. Al-Mubarakpuri's account has him breaking into his sister's house while Khabbab was reciting Surah Ta-Ha, striking her husband, then her, then reading the page and going on to accept Islam. Ibn Sa'd records that Sa'id's wife was a daughter of al-Khattab.
layers.hadith_ref: The Prophet ﷺ of Zayd ibn Amr: 'He died on the religion of Ibrahim' — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III; al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar

layers.title: The Trial
layers.subtitle: He scouted the road to Badr and missed Badr
layers.content:
Ten days before the Prophet ﷺ left Madinah, he sent two men north to find the Quraysh caravan coming from Syria: Talhah ibn Ubaydullah and Sa'id ibn Zayd. No army, no cover — two men riding into the path of the very caravan the Quraysh were arming to protect.

They reached al-Hawra' and stayed there until the caravan went past them. Then the news arrived in Madinah by another route, and the Prophet ﷺ had already set out. The caravan hugged the coast and travelled day and night out of fear of pursuit. Talhah and Sa'id turned for home not knowing any of this, and reached Madinah on the very day the Prophet ﷺ met Quraysh at Badr. They rode out again and met him at Turban, on the road back.

They were not at the battle. The Prophet ﷺ gave them both their shares of the spoils and their reward for Badr, and it was as though they had been present.

Sa'id was at Uhud, at the Ditch and at every expedition afterwards. Later, when Umar as caliph asked the Companions what he could take from the public wealth, Sa'id's answer sided with Uthman's: eat, and feed others.
layers.source: Reported from Haritha al-Ansari and others — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: The tenth name he would not say aloud
layers.content:
Sa'id narrated a hadith and then declined to finish it about himself. The Prophet ﷺ said, 'Be firm, Hira'. There is only a Prophet, a truthful man or a martyr upon you.' Sa'id named nine who were on the mountain: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, Abu Bakr, Umar, Ali, Uthman, Talhah, az-Zubayr, Abd ar-Rahman ibn Awf and Sa'd ibn Malik. Then he stopped. 'If I wished to name the tenth, I would have done it.' He meant himself. In another wording he does list ten of Quraysh promised the Garden, and there he says his own name, alongside Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah.

He died at al-Aqiq outside Madinah in 50 or 51 AH, about seventy years old. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas washed his body. The death was announced on a Friday morning and Ibn Umar left his preparations for Jumu'ah to go to him; he perfumed him, and when asked whether musk should be brought he said, what perfume is sweeter than musk. Sa'd and Ibn Umar climbed down into the grave themselves. Reports differ — the people of Kufa held that he died among them.
layers.hadith_ref: 'Be firm, Hira'. There is only a Prophet, a truthful man or a martyr upon you' — narrated by Sa'id ibn Zayd, Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

quiz.prompt: What did Sa'id's father Zayd ibn Amr do that set him apart from all of Quraysh?

options.text: He became a Christian monk in Syria
He rejected idols and followed the religion of Ibrahim before Islam came
He refused to trade with the Quraysh caravans
He rebuilt the Ka'ba himself

quiz.scholar_reflection: He went to Syria to question the Jews and the Christians, liked neither, and was told by a Christian that what he already believed was the religion of Ibrahim. He answered that the worship of stone or hewn wood is nothing.

quiz.prompt: What did Zayd ibn Amr ask Amir ibn Rabi'a to do for him?

options.text: Look after his son Sa'id
Keep his beliefs secret from Quraysh
Greet the awaited Prophet for him if he lived to see him
Bury him at the foot of Hira'

quiz.citation: Reported from Amir ibn Rabi'a — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Amir became Muslim years later and delivered the greeting. The Prophet ﷺ returned it and prayed for mercy on Zayd, and said he had seen him in the Garden drawing a bucket.

quiz.prompt: What did the Prophet ﷺ say when Umar and Sa'id asked him about Zayd ibn Amr?

options.text: That his case was known only to Allah
That he died on the religion of Ibrahim, and he asked forgiveness and mercy for him
That he should not be mentioned
That he had been sent a Book of his own

quiz.citation: Reported from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ibn Sa'd adds that from that day the Muslims did not mention Zayd without asking mercy for him. A man outside the community by timing was brought inside it by the Prophet's ﷺ own tongue.

quiz.prompt: Why did Sa'id ibn Zayd miss the Battle of Badr?

options.text: He was ill in Madinah
He had been sent north with Talhah to scout the Quraysh caravan
He was still in Makkah
He was guarding the Prophet's ﷺ household

quiz.citation: Reported from Haritha al-Ansari — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: They returned to Madinah on the day the battle was being fought, rode out and met the army coming home. The Prophet ﷺ gave them their shares and their reward as though they had been in the line.

quiz.prompt: In the hadith of Hira' that Sa'id narrated, why did he stop at nine names?

options.text: He had forgotten the tenth
The tenth had not yet accepted Islam
The Prophet ﷺ had named only nine
The tenth was himself

quiz.citation: Reported from Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: His words were: if I wished to name the tenth, I would have done it. He preferred the sentence to be incomplete rather than to say his own name in that list.

quiz.prompt: Zayd was told he probably would not live to see what he was looking for, and kept looking. What do you keep working at without expecting to see the end of it?

options.text: Something for my children or students
A change in my community that will outlast me
Nothing — I need to see results
I have not thought in those terms before

quiz.citation: Reflection on Zayd ibn Amr's message to Amir ibn Rabi'a — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He did not get the meeting. He got the greeting returned, through a friend, after his death. Some work only pays out to the people who come after you.

quiz.prompt: Standing at the Ka'ba, Zayd told Quraysh that none of them was on the truth but him. When have you had to be the only one saying something?

options.text: Often — I am used to it by now
Once or twice, and it cost me
I usually wait until someone else says it first
I avoid situations that would require it

quiz.citation: Reported from Asma bint Abi Bakr — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He said it in the most public place in Arabia, with his back to the building itself. There is no record of anyone agreeing with him that day.

quiz.prompt: Sa'id did the dangerous reconnaissance and was absent from the battle everyone remembers. How do you handle work that no one sees you doing?

options.text: It genuinely does not bother me
It bothers me and I try not to show it
I make sure the right people know
I gravitate to visible work instead

quiz.citation: Reflection on the scouting mission to al-Hawra' — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Prophet ﷺ settled it by giving him the share and the reward of a man who had fought. The record was corrected even though the story could not be.

quiz.prompt: Zayd took infant girls off men who were going to bury them, and raised them at his own cost. What wrong in front of you have you taken on personally?

options.text: Something I paid for out of my own pocket
Something I spoke against but did not act on
Something I decided was not mine to fix
I have not been in that position

quiz.citation: Reported from Asma bint Abi Bakr — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: His words to the father were plain: take it easy, do not kill her, I will support her for you. When the girl was grown he offered her back, and offered to keep her. He had thought past the rescue.

quiz.prompt: Sa'id would not say his own name in a list of ten promised Paradise. What do you do when you are being counted among people you admire?

options.text: Accept it and try to be worth it
Deflect it, sometimes too hard
Quietly enjoy it
Assume they have misjudged me

quiz.citation: Reported from Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He did name himself in another narration of the same promise. He was not denying it — he was declining to be the one who said it.
